4. DEFINING ‘^AGENCY ACTION”
Section 702 of the APA entitles “a person suffering a legal wrong 
because of agency action, or adversely affected or aggrieved by agency 
action * * * to judicial review.” Thus, those who have suffered harm as a 
result of agency action are entitled to review. “Agency action’ is defined in 
section 551 as including; “the whole or part of an agency rule, order, license, 
sanction, relief, or the equivalent or denial thereof, or failure to act.” In 
many cases, it will be clear that an agency action has taken place because 
an agency will issue an order or promulgate a rule.
In other cases, however, “agency action” is not so clear. Agencies 
engage in a host of other types of regulatory activities that do not invoke 
their formal law making or enforcement authority. Plaintiffs challenging 
these sorts of “managerial” or “informal” regulatory processes must 
demonstrate not only that the agency is required to act, but that the act 
that is required is one that counts as “agency action for purposes of the 
judicial review provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act. 
Additionally, as section 551 states, agency inaction can quahfy as “agency 
action” for the purposes of judicial review. When petitioners seek the 
promulgation of a particular rule or the initiation of enforcement 
proceedings they seek to force agencies to begin one of the two formal 
processes, adjudication or rulemaking, through which agencies make law. 
In most of these attempts to force an agency’s hand, the critical question is 
whether the applicable statutes require agency action and therefore 
provide criteria by which a court can determine whether the agency s 
failure to act is proper.
